title: Generalizable and Scalable Robot Learning in the Physical World | EECS at UC Berkeley
content: Generalizable and Scalable Robot Learning in the Physical World | EECS at UC Berkeley Generalizable and Scalable Robot Learning in the Physical World Fangchen Liu EECS Department, University of California, Berkeley Technical Report No. UCB/EECS-2026-4 January 12, 2026 http://www2.eecs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/TechRpts/2026/EECS-2026-4.pdf Foundation models in vision and language have demonstrated strong generalization capabilities by leveraging internet-scale data with scalable training recipes. In contrast, robot policies still face fundamental challenges in robustness, reliability, and generalization when deployed in the unseen real-world scenarios. A key limiting factor is the scarcity of large-scale, diverse, and high-quality robot data. Unlike vision-language datasets, physical robot data is expensive and slow to collect and more difficult to parallelize. These challenges create a fundamental gap between the data and training regimes that enable success in vision-language foundation models and those currently available for robot learning. This dissertation investigates scalable and generalizable approaches toward robot foundation models by improving how robotic learning systems acquire, represent, and utilize data. It argues that progress toward robust robot foundation models requires advances along three complementary directions: (i) effectively leveraging heterogeneous data sources, including internet-scale vision-language data, exploratory or suboptimal sensorimotor trajectories, and high-quality demonstrations; (ii) developing data-efficient and generalizable policy models; and (iii) designing scalable real-world data collection systems that reduce the cost of acquiring demonstrations. Following these perspectives, this thesis presents a set of algorithmic and systems contributions toward building robot foundation models, spanning learning beyond demonstrations for low-level sensorimotor skills and high-level task reasoning, designing more generalizable robotic policies, and developing scalable real-world data collection systems. First, it introduces MaskDP, the first framework that unifies world modeling and decision prediction from exploratory sensorimotor trajectories, enabling diverse downstream behaviors. Second, it presents MOKA, which leverages pretrained vision-language models for robotic manipulation by grounding tasks into a structured set of visual keypoints and waypoints. Third, it introduces OTTER, a vision-language-action policy that interfaces pretrained vision-language representations with action prediction, preserving generalization across instructions, objects, and environments while enabling precise and data-efficient control. This dissertation also revisits early attempts at in-context policy learning through one-shot imitation, where policies condition on demonstrations as context. Finally, it presents Vitamin, a scalable and portable system for collecting high-quality real-world demonstrations using improved tactile sensing and teleoperation interfaces, enabling learning for contact-rich manipulation tasks. Together, these contributions demonstrate how scalable robot learning can emerge from combining heterogeneous data sources, generalizable learning algorithms, and scalable data acquisition systems. Overall, this dissertation bridges representation learning, policy learning, and data collection, advancing robot foundation models toward reliable performance in practical real-world settings.
